scope: Twelfth expansion batch: 15 exercises. Three wari assessments, three explicitly marked kuse reproaches, six shared sue/ageku eventual-outcome items with three model options per noun, and three additional ue items. The six shared answers do not measure independent discrimination between sue and ageku.

sources.publisher: Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten via Kotobank
sources.section: Wari noun [二] sense 8: the degree naturally expected from a person or thing's character/state, in ...wari ni (wa). The entry supplies 割 and 割り notation. This is not the percentage-counter sense or the separate warito adverb.

Assessment relative to an expected standard; na-adjective + na and noun + no. The broad claim that comparisons can only be with the same category and the historical/suffix generalizations are not adopted.

sources.publisher: Daijisen and Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten via Kotobank
sources.section: Inspected actual HTML, not the simplified extraction that omits the entry. Daijisen's くせに【癖に】 defines a contrast with reproach/dissatisfaction, with attributive-form or noun + no attachment, and compares its stronger reproach with no ni. The adjacent dictionary entry also explicitly includes criticism. This supports a marked reproach construction, not the claim that other constructions cannot be critical in context.

Inspected actual HTML: すえ【末】 sense 5, after a process, with examples ごたごたの末落ち着く and 苦心の末完成した. It does not restrict sue to favorable outcomes. The simplified extraction omits this modern entry and instead exposes other readings and the historical dictionary.

A negative result after substantial effort/time, or a troublesome process even if the ultimate result is not bad; past-verb and noun + no attachment. The spelling note supplies 挙句 and 挙げ句. No global rule that every outcome must be bad is adopted.

Entry with spellings 挙句 and 揚げ句, reading あげく; first sense after a long process/at its end, usually after a plain past verb or noun + no, also with ni. The final-renga-line sense is not the construction being practiced.

Inspected actual HTML heading あげ‐く【挙（げ）句／揚（げ）句】 and adverbial result sense 3. Optional げ in both written forms also supports 揚句. Only the Daijisen entry is used, not the adjacent expression dictionary or automatically generated examples. This establishes spelling recognition, not equal frequency.
Additive ue ni, with plain verbs/i-adjectives, na-adjective + na and noun + no. The past-verb additive item is not reclassified as an eventual outcome solely because it has a completed verb.

authoringNotes: All examples are newly authored and need independent linguistic review. Source recognition of a spelling is not a claim of equal frequency or automatic collocational naturalness.

The wari/kuse questions visibly restrict the noun list and framing. Wari items exclude a mocking/reproachful tone, including teasing praise with kuse. Kuse items specifically ask for the construction conventionally marking reproach itself; context alone can make wari or no ni critical too. Do not remove these restrictions and claim unrestricted single-answer discrimination.

Wari covers i-adjective, noun + no and past-verb attachment. Kuse covers nonpast/ongoing verb clauses and noun + no. Na-adjective connections are explained in the article but not separate targets in these six exercises.

All six process outcomes deliberately allow both sue and ageku in one answer class: four verb-clause and two event-noun frames, all following effort or difficulty and ending unfavorably. There are three sue model buttons and three ageku model buttons, not six independent noun-discrimination items.

The outcome/addition questions visibly request sue, ageku or ue with printed ni, and state the intended relation. Ato and other outcome expressions can work in other formulations; ue de is a different supplied-particle frame. These are not globally wrong alternatives.
This batch does not make sue positive-only or ageku bad-result-only, and does not claim to cover every sue/ageku sense. Its shared outcome tasks do not separately practice favorable outcomes.

All prior 155 exercise records remain unchanged against preservationBaseline: 62 from the committed tree and 93 in six files whose raw SHA256 hashes were recorded before this batch. One SRS identity per exercise, not per noun spelling, model option or choose/type presentation.
